source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Blood type (A, B, AB, O) is measured at which level?
questions.rationale: Nominal measurement classifies attributes into mutually exclusive categories with no order.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 364)
questions.quote: nominal measurement—the classification of attributes into mutually exclusive categories

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Pain rated as mild, moderate or severe is measured at which level?
questions.rationale: Ordinal measurement ranks people by relative standing; distances between ranks are not equal.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 364)
questions.quote: ordinal measurement—the ranking of people based on their relative standing on an attribute

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Body temperature in degrees Celsius is measured at the interval level because it:
options: It has a true zero point
questions.rationale: Interval scales show rank and distance; ratio scales (e.g., weight) also have a rational zero.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 364)
questions.quote: ratio measurement—distinguished from interval measurement by having a rational zero point.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which is measured at the ratio level?
questions.rationale: Weight has equal intervals and a true zero; 0 kg means no weight.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 364)
questions.quote: ratio measurement—distinguished from interval measurement by having a rational zero point.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: The ages of five mothers are 18, 20, 20, 25 and 32. What is the mode?
questions.rationale: The mode is the value that occurs most often (20). The mean is 23 and the median is 20.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 364)
questions.quote: The mode is the value that occurs most frequently

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Hospital stays (days) of seven patients: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 20. Which measure best describes the typical stay?
questions.rationale: The median (middle value) is not distorted by the extreme value of 20; the mean is pulled upward.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 364)
questions.quote: the median is the point above which and below which 50% of the cases fall

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which index of central tendency is the most stable?
questions.rationale: The mean is the most stable measure of central tendency.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 364)
questions.quote: The mean is the most stable index of central tendency.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which statistic shows how much, on average, scores deviate from the mean?
questions.rationale: The standard deviation is an index of variability; the range is highest minus lowest score.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 365)
questions.quote: The standard deviation (SD) indicates how much, on average, scores deviate from the mean.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: In a normal (bell-shaped) distribution, about what percentage of values fall within 2 SDs of the mean?
questions.rationale: About 95% of values lie within ±2 SDs of the mean (about 68% within ±1 SD).
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 365)
questions.quote: In a normal distribution, 95% of values lie within 2 SDs above and below the mean.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A study reports r = −0.85 between hours of exercise and body weight. This means:
questions.rationale: Correlation ranges from −1 to +1; −0.85 is strong and inverse (more exercise, lower weight). It does not prove causation.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 365)
questions.quote: range from −1.00 (perfect negative correlation) through .00 to +1.00 (perfect positive correlation).

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which correlation coefficient is used when both variables are continuous (interval or ratio)?
questions.rationale: Pearson's r is for continuous variables; Spearman's rho is for ordinal data.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 365)
questions.quote: The most frequently used correlation coefficient is Pearson’s r, used with continuous variables.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A researcher compares the mean blood pressure of two groups: one given a low-salt diet and one given a usual diet. The appropriate test is the:
questions.rationale: The t-test compares two group means; ANOVA is used for three or more groups.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 366)
questions.quote: Two common statistical tests are the t-test and analysis of variance (ANOVA), both of which can be used to test the significance of the difference between group means

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Mean pain scores of patients in three different wards are compared. The appropriate test is:
questions.rationale: ANOVA is used when comparing means of three or more groups.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 366)
questions.quote: ANOVA is used when there are three or more groups.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A researcher compares the proportion of smokers among male and female students. The appropriate test is:
questions.rationale: Chi-square tests differences in proportions (categorical data).
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 366)
questions.quote: The chi-squared test is used to test hypotheses about group differences in proportions.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A study reports p = 0.03 with alpha set at 0.05. The researcher should:
options: Conclude the result is due to chance
questions.rationale: When p is below alpha (0.05), the result is statistically significant and the null hypothesis is rejected.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 366)
questions.quote: statistically significant means that the obtained results are not likely to be due to chance fluctuations at a given probability (p value).

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A researcher concludes a new drug works when, in truth, it has no effect. This is a:
questions.rationale: A Type I error is wrongly rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive); Type II is wrongly accepting a false null (false negative).
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 366)
questions.quote: A Type I error occurs if a null hypothesis is wrongly rejected (false positives).

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A small study finds no significant effect of a program that truly works. This is a Type II error, and the best way to reduce it is to:
questions.rationale: Power (ability to detect true effects) increases with sample size; 0.80 is the usual acceptable power.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 366)
questions.quote: Power increases as sample size increases.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: The conventional level of significance (alpha) in nursing research is:
questions.rationale: Alpha of 0.05 means a 5% risk of a Type I error; 0.80 is the usual standard for power.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 366)
questions.quote: The .05 level (the conventional standard)

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A study reports a mean hemoglobin of 11.2 g/dL with a 95% confidence interval of 10.8–11.6. This interval means:
options: True mean likely in this range
All patients fall in this range
questions.rationale: A 95% CI gives the range within which the true population value is expected to fall, with 95% probability.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 365)
questions.quote: there is a 95% probability that the true population value lies between the upper and lower confidence limits.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A screening test correctly identifies 90% of people who truly have TB. This property is its:
questions.rationale: Sensitivity is the rate of true positives; specificity is the rate of true negatives.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 367)
questions.quote: Sensitivity is the instrument’s ability to identify a case correctly (i.e., its rate of yielding true positives).

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A dengue rapid test correctly gives a negative result for 95% of people who do not have dengue. This is its:
questions.rationale: Specificity is the ability to identify non-cases correctly (true negatives).
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 367)
questions.quote: Specificity is the instrument’s ability to identify noncases correctly (i.e., its rate of yielding true negatives).

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Descriptive statistics are used to:
questions.rationale: Descriptive statistics summarize data; inferential statistics draw conclusions about populations from samples.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 364)
questions.quote: Descriptive statistics are used to summarize and describe quantitative data.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A drug lowers blood pressure by 1 mmHg with p < 0.001 in a very large study. The nurse recognizes that the result is:
questions.rationale: Clinical significance is the practical importance of results in patients' lives; large samples can make tiny effects statistically significant.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 15 Summary (PDF p. 389)
questions.quote: clinical significance refers to the practical importance of research results

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Repeating a study in another hospital and getting the same results is called:
questions.rationale: Corroboration through replication strengthens confidence in results.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 15 Summary (PDF p. 389)
questions.quote: Corroboration (replication) of results, through either internal or external sources

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Statistically combining the results of several randomized trials into one overall effect estimate is a:
questions.rationale: Meta-analysis integrates quantitative findings statistically; metasynthesis integrates qualitative findings.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 18 Summary (PDF p. 453)
questions.quote: Systematic reviews of quantitative studies often involve statistical integration of findings in a meta-analysis

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Studies with nonsignificant results are less likely to be published, which can make a meta-analysis overestimate effects. This is:
questions.rationale: Publication bias from underreporting of nonsignificant findings can inflate pooled effects; including grey literature helps.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 18 Summary (PDF p. 453)
questions.quote: publication bias stemming from the underrepresentation of nonsignificant findings in published reports can lead to overestimates of effects.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Statistics that allow a researcher to draw conclusions about a population from a sample are:
questions.rationale: Inferential statistics, based on probability, estimate population parameters from sample data.
questions.source: Polit & Beck, Essentials of Nursing Research, 9th ed. (2018), Ch. 14 Summary (PDF p. 365)
questions.quote: Inferential statistics, based on laws of probability, allow researchers to make inferences about population parameters based on data from a sample.
